speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I beg leave to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head P of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our officers under the command of Col Chew Keng Tok, were activated to fly to Türkiye at short notice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There, for 10 days, they operated in very difficult conditions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They had to contend with freezing temperatures, the ever-present threat of the further collapse of buildings and the calamitous security situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, rescue officers from several other countries suspended their operations owing to the prevailing security situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They saved lives, comforted many and brought honour to our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That our officers were able to execute their duties, in such a way as to win the admiration of the Turkish people, is a testimony to their sterling standard of training and preparedness, strong sense of duty and purpose, excellent leadership and high morale.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From the reports that I have read, I note that our SCDF officers' work was enabled by the technology of our Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) equipment, such as fibre-optic scopes to detect lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is clear to me that technology has, and will, continue to play an increasingly important role in securing better outcomes in operations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are a number of factors that drive this, including the reality that our Home Team's manpower is likely to remain lean and the likelihood that our Singaporeans will constantly expect more of the Home Team over time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must, in short, do more with less.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Over the years, the Home Team has invested heavily on technology.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) officers leverage on video analytics and live tracking technology to maintain security at the Woodlands and Tuas checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Singapore Prison Service (SPS) is trialling an unmanned and automated urine collection and screening system for its prison inmates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What has been the tangible returns from these investments?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And what would be the framework under which further investments will be made?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also wish to understand how the Home Team Science and Technology Agency, set up in 2019, has aided the development of cost-effective science and technological capabilities for our Home Team operations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, I wish to better understand how the Police's effectiveness is being measured.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Several decades back, the Police relied on the prevalence of the five preventable crimes as a measure of its effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Over time, these key performance indicators (KPIs) became less relevant with the emergence of new kinds of crime, such as internet-based scams.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had previously suggested that the Police publish how much it has seized pursuant to criminal investigations and how much is returned to victims of crime as a KPI.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is done in the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, it appears to me that there is an ability to track such data.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I alluded to in my preceding paragraphs, even as I speak about the need for technology, I also see that there remains an irreducible human dimension in keeping Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must ensure that our investment in developing our Home Team's human capital is kept in tandem too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is the hon Minister's plan in this regard?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me, by reference to the increasing number of recent cases of young persons being self-radicalised through access to harmful online content, that there is a case to take a relook at the legislative levers to ensure that our Home Team officers, particularly the Internal Security Department (ISD), have the tools to prevent the proliferation of such cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, the impact on Singapore can be significant and severe.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should remind ourselves that terrorists need only be successful once.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: ISD, on the other hand, has to be successful all the time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2022, it was announced in this House that the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) will develop a framework that will tackle online criminal activity, including content inciting violence in our community, to complement the current legislative measures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seek an update on this matter, please.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I commend the SPS for spearheading efforts with its stakeholders to keep the recidivism rate amongst desistors relatively low and stable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I think, from the experience of the JGI and the steps taken by SPS, we have an opportunity to aim for even lower recidivism rates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In turn, by being gainfully employed in good jobs that have good prospects, it gives our desistors the best chance to break free from their past.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To effect permanent changes, we have to start with the individual and work with their families too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will not be easy, but it has to be done.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The purpose is to motivate desistors to be responsible family members and encourage reconciliation within their families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I truly believe that once our desistors are accepted back and reconciled with their families, the sky will be the limit for them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a broader point, our community must play its part to encourage our desistors to make strong contributions to their families and enrich the Singapore story.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They have talent, knowledge and experience which Singapore can benefit from.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to get behind them and signal to them that we will support them, so long as they keep on the path of rehabilitation and reintegration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Early last year, I suggested in this House that our desistors be given an opportunity to perform at our National Day Parade.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Having seen them perform, I know that they will be a hit amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understood that my suggestion was made too late for National Day Parade (NDP) 2022.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder whether it will be in time for NDP 2023 instead.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also need to pay special attention to desistors with drug-abusing pasts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that this is the group of persons who are more likely to reoffend as they struggle to steer clear from the triggers that made them consume drugs in the first place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I have spoken on what I see to be the three elements of securing Singapore for the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Courage is beyond price, but technology and developing the talents of our men and women in the Home Team, these require constant investments and our continued support.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I look forward to hearing from the Minister and her colleagues on the issues that I have raised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In line with the Government's Forward Singapore (Forward SG) exercise that promises a renewed social compact with citizens, we need to ask: what should Singapore's goals be when bringing in new citizens?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We want those who truly know Singapore and want to embrace the Singaporean way of life.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We want those who really want to live here and be here.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We want people who have already proven themselves by having integrated into the Singaporean life after some time as Permanent Residents (PRs).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans do not want new citizens who do not want to live here, but only want the power of the Singapore passport for their convenience, and the safe and secure environment for their assets and wealth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We do not want new citizens who are reluctant for their sons to do National Service (NS) and, certainly, none of us want people who only want Singapore Citizenship as a stepping-stone to another country but, instead, seek those who have a long-term commitment to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has promised that Forward SG will move on to looking at solutions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Swiss, for example, have a highly specific selection process for new citizens.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: People must show deep commitment before granted Swiss citizenship through naturalisation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Applicants must show themselves to be successfully integrated into Switzerland and know the Swiss ways and customs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For ordinary naturalisation, a person must have lived in Switzerland for 10 years and hold a permanent residence permit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Swiss Naturalisation Authorities summon applicants for a personal interview which focuses on their knowledge of Switzerland.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They must be able to answer questions on Swiss geography, history, politics and society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is the working proficiency in English a criterion for citizenship for better integration between new citizens and Singaporeans of all races and religion, since English is our main language of communication?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government share more details on how new citizenships are granted, as there are aspects of the process and criteria currently that are opaque?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How is our system different from that of the Swiss?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is there already a point system in place and what does it consider apart from the publicly revealed criteria, such as economic contribution, educational qualification, family profile and length of stay in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Most importantly, how will the citizenship selection process evolve in face of the Forward SG exercise and a review of the social compact?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Police have described the two categories as cyber-enabled offences and cyber dependent offences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Cyber dependent offences are those where digital assets are the target and includes hacking, ransomware and website defacements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These of these offences are covered by the Computer Misuse Act.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, cyber-enabled crimes relate to crimes that are facilitated by the computer and include the wide range of scams, cyber harassment, cyber extortion and illegal online gambling.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are currently covered by different pieces of legislation, including the Penal Code and the Protection from Harassment Act.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While there are a wide range of tools that are needed to deal with such crimes, legislation is obviously an important component.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Does MHA see any gaps in the existing legislative framework to deal with cybercrime?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the Committee of Supply (COS) debate in 2022, MHA mentioned that it was working on a framework to deal with a broad suite of online criminal activity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: How will this framework relate to the existing legislation?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to continually strengthen our technological capability, so as to detect crime, including multi-jurisdictional crimes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is the Home Team doing to leverage on technology to battle domestic and transnational crime, and does this requires some degree of transformation of operations?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: MHA fulfils a key function: the maintenance of order and law in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But with declining birth rates, manpower has been, and will continue to be, affected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Leveraging on technology, cooperation with the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF), partnerships with international organisations such as Interpol and good relationships with Police forces in the region are key to making up for the reducing pool of local manpower.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But in the round, manpower is still key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ground, human judgement is key in ground ops and, therefore, how will MHA transform itself to ensure: one, that our officers continue to be world-class; and two, that our world-class officers work alongside best-in-class technology to assist in the fight against crime?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The teenagers were contacts of another self-radicalised 18-year-old, who was also detained by ISD last December.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although they were self-radicalised separately, they subsequently became acquainted online.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The teenagers joined multiple extremist-themed servers on the online gaming platform Roblox.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such online gaming platforms are being used by extremist groups to disseminate their ideological beliefs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They use video games and gaming culture to attract and influence our youths.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to keep abreast of the technological developments and current societal trends, to prevent terrorists from abusing such online platforms to spread extremist ideologies that prey on the minds of our youths.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can MHA provide an update on how it intends to tackle this trend?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With the threat of self-radicalisation becoming more apparent in Singapore and around the region, stepping up our efforts in countering the threat of terrorism is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We need to continually strengthen our regulatory framework and our detection capabilities, so as to keep a close watch on potential terror situations or threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How will MHA continue to partner with other states in our fight against terrorism, given that the fight is not one that exists in vacuum?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Further, how is the Home Team transforming its operational capabilities, such as to prevent terrorist financing and to prevent money laundering in relation to terrorism?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: However, there is a gradually growing perception that drugs are less harmful or not harmful if used just socially.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But it is obvious that experimental drug use can lead to addiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How does MHA intend to reinvent and transform its engagements and messages regarding the growing tolerance to drugs?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In particular, how will MHA explain that the liberalisation of recreational drug use in other countries, including those in the region, will in every likelihood lead to massive long-term societal harm?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Such brutally honest messaging could achieve the deterrent effect needed to puncture the growing tolerance to drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Youths form a significant proportion of new abusers of illicit drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We need to continue and readily impart drug-free values to the next generation, and educate and inculcate the understanding that addiction is not without consequences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Families can be torn apart by addiction and what is more, widespread addiction can lead to devastating consequences on our society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How does MHA intend to ramp up its engagement of our youths regarding the dangers of drug abuse, especially in the light of the growing and dangerous lure of cannabis?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, I support our zero-tolerance stance against drugs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unfortunately, as some other countries resort to legalising and decriminalising drugs, such a liberal attitude towards narcotics has been spreading through social media and other channels.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This may have an impact on certain segments of our society, including some youths.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will MHA proceed with its efforts to prevent drug abuse?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This could be because former offenders are more likely to fall in with bad company and into their old ways once Government support tapers off.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Yellow Ribbon Singapore (YRSG) looks at rebuilding the lives of former inmates and ex-offenders through skills and career development.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are excellent programmes, like training even before an inmate is released and career coaching.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister elaborate on MHA and YRSG's plans in the coming year for programmes specifically targeting the two- to five-year period after an ex-offender for drug offences has been released?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It appears from the statistics that this is an important period to have ongoing programmes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, recidivism should be tackled not only through helping ex-offenders get jobs, but through community support as well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: YRSG held its second CARE Network Summit in 2022.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Could I ask the Minister to elaborate on what outcomes from that summit will be implemented by YRSG this year, or that YRSG is considering?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: How will community groups and employers be involved?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to ask, Sir, how does YRSG actively reach out and provide support to families of offenders and ex-offenders, and could the Minister elaborate on YRSG's plans for this year in this area?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Drug laws, Sir, has been liberalised in many countries, including neighbouring countries.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Could I ask the Minister, how would the Government ameliorate the effect of a stepped-up anti-drug campaign on ex-offenders, such that we do not see a resurgence of stigmatisation?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: As a Board Member of YRSG, I am proud of all the efforts made by the entire ecosystem of support from the SPS, MHA, community partners and employers to assist us in the reintegration effort.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: As mentioned in my COS speech last year, we need "offenders" to become "overcomers" – overcoming the challenges in life in a whole-of-society approach.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I welcome that SPS now use the term "desistors", which helps to remove the stigma of incarceration.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: How does MHA intend to further reduce the long-term recidivism rates of ex-offenders?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: By raising more awareness to accept former offenders as fellow and equal members of society, we can generate greater public support which could translate into a greater number of volunteers for the Community Action for the Rehabilitation of Ex-offenders (CARE) Network, the Yellow Ribbon Project and other aftercare programmes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is MHA creating awareness and generating acceptance for our former offenders, in order to facilitate their transition and welcoming back into society?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Such a welcoming attitude will also reduce the chance of re-offending and, possibly, even heal families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In the road to recovery and reintegration, mentorship is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How can MHA and the SPS continue to enhance the provision of post-release mentorship schemes for our former offenders?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Chairman, I have met Clementi residents who are ex-offenders.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some were in prison for many years, and upon release, find that the job market has changed from the days before.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some are older, having been in and out of incarceration and now are dealing with health conditions, even as they are trying to find work.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Finding work, finding a job – it is part of the recovery journey, the rehabilitation journey, rebuilding a life while coming back into society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What is MHA doing to improve the employability of ex-offenders who are rebuilding their lives, and how are we recognising employers who are inclusive, employers who lean in to give someone that second chance in life?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As part of our #EveryWorkerMatters conversation exercise last month, together with my National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) colleagues and volunteers, I had the great opportunity to host a dialogue session at our NTUC premises for more than 100 employers, ex-offenders, YRSG, SPS and New Charis Mission friends.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is the first time that NTUC and the Labour Movement has engaged this community for a dialogue.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On another occasion earlier this month, my team and I had an opportunity to engage a group of inmates at Changi Prison as part of our #EveryWorkerMatters conversation to share as well as hear their thoughts on jobs, training, skills and employment and employability in general.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I applaud the work of YRSG and SPS and for making our engagement possible, so that we can hear first-hand from the community as we forge a new workers' compact.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As much as it was happy to hear some employers leaning forward to help and hire ex-offenders, we hear the fears and anxieties from the inmates who are soon to be released and wanting to reintegrate back into society as well as find decent work when they are out.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this respect, I wish to make three points.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, I wish to know what is being done thus far and the plans of SPS and YRSG in this important space to help in the employment and employability needs of ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This area has not been reviewed for a long time and I hope the review will be able to give ex-offenders a higher chance of employment and employability when they re-enter into the workforce and society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This statistic shows that efforts by CNB and our community, through the close cooperation of the Dadah Is Haram Campaign, M3 and other Malay/Muslim bodies, have yielded results.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Our Malay/Muslim community has also greatly supported the Dadah Is Haram Campaign through a network of more than 70 mosques throughout Singapore and volunteers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Apart from that, the FITRAH program by M3 and our Malay/Muslim Organisations Rehabilitation Network have also helped to combat the scourge of drugs and its impact on our community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Chairman, therefore, I would like to ask what is MHA's plan to continue working with our Malay/Muslim community to help offenders and ex-offenders within our community?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Let us ensure that our security officers are not left behind in all this talk of work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, the recent statistics that were released by the Police on scams has surely captured our attention on the threat that scams are causing in the community.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: That the Police released this set of statistics separate and distinct from other crime numbers for the first time, shows that scams are fast becoming a major cause of concern.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And for those of us who think that seniors are generally the vulnerable class in society that are more susceptible to being scammed, we know that the cases involving seniors only amount to 8.8% of all cases.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Anecdotally, I am sure all of us have heard of many stories of scams.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As representatives in this House, we will also have met many residents who have sought our assistance when scammed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Not so long ago, I remember that the concern was mainly about phishing links, sent by emails, digital messages or on social media.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Raising awareness on such modus operandi was easier.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We warned one another not to click on links immediately, to always question and verify before proceeding.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There are now scams that appear to be innocuous, but end up being most insidious.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Scammers masquerade as love interests, friends who have changed numbers and are in need of assistance, or even promise what appeared to be legitimate jobs but end up cheating, often times, the life savings of individuals.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Some scams even play the long game for many months, slowly cheating not only money, but also causing great emotional turmoil to its victims.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Perhaps, what is the most alarming about scams, is the fact that it is often the case that these scams originate from overseas, and once money is transferred to another account, it promptly leaves our shores and jurisdiction almost instantaneously.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This makes the task of the Police, no matter how well-trained and determined they are, all the more challenging in arresting scammers and, especially, in their efforts to retrieve the stolen monies for the victims.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premise, I invite the Minister to share with this House, the steps that the Government is taking to address the threat of scams in the community, whether the Ministry has plans to strengthen legislation to combat scams and the efforts that are being made to educate and keep the public informed of the latest developments, so that Singaporeans can take the necessary precautions against scams.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, scam victims suffer more than just financial losses.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It often takes a toll on them physically, mentally and socially.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Many may be too embarrassed to seek help.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Victims feel anxiety, shame and helplessness, and a variety of other emotions which may lead to depression, tension and stress.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The deep shame may also prevent these victims from seeking help.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They may also engage in self-harm or turn suicidal.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Building on that, could I also suggest having a one-stop unit that collaborates with relevant agencies and professionals dedicated to assisting scam victims amid a scam, or after they have fallen prey to the scam?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This unit could ensure that vulnerable groups, such as the deaf – who may not be able to utilise the phone hotlines – can get timely help.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Post-scam, frontline officers from the Police or banks could refer victims to this "Post-Scam" Unit to better address their financial and mental needs promptly.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Financially, the unit can assess the victim's financial needs, provide information about financial support services and refer the victim to relevant social service agencies.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Emotionally, the Post-Scam Unit would be equipped to assess their mental health needs and provide immediate emotional support, if needed, to prevent further deterioration in their mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The unit can then refer the victim to follow-up mental health services and support groups.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They can also provide updates on the status of the investigation and any support services that may be available to the victim.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you can take your four cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Laws need to be regularly reviewed to respond to the fast-evolving nature of the scams.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There needs to be sufficient flexibility within the legislation and subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: People are being lured by easy money to sell their Singpass details and bank accounts for purposes, such as money laundering, facilitating unauthorised access to computer material and carrying out unlicensed businesses.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is MHA aiming to reduce the prevalence of money mule accounts and lower the incidence of people selling their personal details and bank accounts?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To build a strong digital infrastructure to prevent scams, we need to utilise technology, such as big data, to be able to spot common patterns, to highlight suspicious transactions and websites with scammers spoofing e-commerce platforms, fake friend call scams and impersonation scams.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is MHA using technology and partnering with various stakeholders to further flag out suspicious transactions, for our digital infrastructure needs to develop, to put up more barriers and warnings against phishing and other forms of data theft?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This includes not just Government agencies and banks, but telcos' customers and consumers, and the community at large.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is the Government working in tandem with the various sectors, in order to develop specific and targeted approaches to dealing with different sorts of scams particularly, because scams evolve quickly?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What infrastructure is in place to respond to new forms of scams across the various industries, such that all stakeholders are informed and play their part in collectively combatting the threat?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In recent years, there has been a proliferation of scams, including e-commerce scams, Internet love scams and investment scams.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These scams are particularly difficult to track and counter, because these deal with daily life and, to some extent, human sentiment and human emotion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Given how fast scams can evolve and new scams can appear, we need to be able to quickly inform the public, especially the targeted groups that are most vulnerable to a particular form of scam.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is the Government working to continually update the public on new forms of scams, and keeping up with its public education and awareness efforts?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, earlier this month, the Police released data on cybercrime which was reported by CNA, and the figures were sobering.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The top five scam types were phishing scams, job scams, e-commerce scams, investment scams and fake friend call scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: They made up about 80% of the top 10 scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: It is good that the Police is keeping tracks and close tabs on cybercrime data and able to produce such information on the issue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I am interested to know what steps are being taken to combat cybercrime, and whether the existing steps are enough.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In particular, I wonder whether the Police believe any further steps need to be taken in educating the public better, as well as steps that are required to catch and prosecute the perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Where these perpetrators are abroad, which I believe happens in many of the scams, have we had any success in capturing the perpetrators and/or recovering assets for victims?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Derrick Goh, you can take your earlier cut as well.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, I mentioned in our Budget debate about the worrying trend we are seeing, where youths perpetuating crimes is on the increase.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On the scams front, SPF reported that a majority of those arrested for e-commerce scams were youths.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While Singapore has been steadfast in its zero-tolerance approach towards drugs, even amid more liberal attitudes towards the use of drugs both internationally and in the region, such as in Thailand, CNB has also highlighted a worrying trend of more youths abusing cannabis.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is complicated by the continued emergence of new psychoactive substances and a quadrupling of vaping cases from 2020 to 2022.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Such illicit habits appeal more to the youth and could be gateways to other forms of harder substance abuse, as well as give rise to other social ills and offences.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Moreover, accessibility to these harms is easily facilitated in the digital space, where youths can deal anonymously, which could be challenging for our agencies to detect.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What is equally concerning is that in most cases, parents did not seem to be aware of their child's involvement with such harms.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Can MHA explain its plans on how it can deepen engagement with all stakeholders in the ecosystem – parents, schools, youth groups, media platforms, and so on, to identify at-risk youths for more timely and effective intervention?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What further measures will MHA take to address this worrying trend of youth perpetrating crimes?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Despite the increased and commendable efforts by MHA and its partners, the scourge of scams remains unabated and continues to evolve.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This means that in the past two years, close to over S$1.3 billion has been lost to scams.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A discerning public is our first line of defence.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: MHA has been strengthening public education efforts, through the ACT Against Scams campaign and by encouraging residents to download the ScamShield app.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Noteworthy, is the step up in anti-scam enforcements, such as the recent island-wide operation in February, where over 500 scammers and money mules were arrested.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Unlike physical crimes, scams are perpetrated by highly organised transnational syndicates and conducted swiftly in the digital space; and experts have also spoken about sophisticated operations that are aided by AI.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Combatting scams, hence, requires a concerted "all-hands-on-deck" response.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: MHA should build upon its success to further deepen international co-operation with foreign law enforcement agencies, and partnerships with stakeholders like, for example, platform providers, communication and social media firms, as well as e-commerce players in the digital value chain.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To be effective, these stakeholders, who themselves benefit and profit from the digital ecosystem, need to do more and have accountability clearly assigned, to drive more proactive upstream prevention of scams.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This will become important as recent trends show that while the number of scams have increased, the amount lost per transaction is smaller on average.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This trend is expected to worsen as frictionless payments increase along with more cross-border linkages, such as the link-up of Singapore's PayNow with Thailand's PromptPay and, as announced last week, India's UPI.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We are an international and well-digitalised financial centre.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: There is a pressing need for us to swiftly and resolutely act against scams to uphold public trust, as the digital world becomes more complex with greater cybersecurity risks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has often been lauded as one of the safest cities in the world, and we should uphold this standing in the digital sphere too.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, at the outset, let me thank Mr Murali Pillai and Members for their recognition of our SCDF officers, as well as the team behind Operation Lionheart.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They have done us proud and in a very tragic situation, we are glad that Singapore was able to make a small contribution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since 2015, we have been ranked first in Gallup's Global Law and Order Report, except in 2021, when the survey was not conducted here due to the pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the 2022 World Justice Project Rule of Law Index, Singapore was ranked as one of the top three countries in "order and security", for the sixth time in a row.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These accolades do not mean that we can take our peaceful state of affairs for granted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the contrary, given the dynamic operating environment, the Home Team is constantly challenged with emerging threats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include foreign interferences, scams and other cybercrimes, and a more permissive global attitude towards drugs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: My MHA colleagues and I will share how we are responding to these challenges, and also address points raised by Members.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Minister of State Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim will speak on our efforts to combat drug abuse, including by enhancing our rehabilitation programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Minister of State Sun Xueling will speak on our multi-pronged approach to tackle scams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will speak about online crimes more generally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have been able to keep our country safe and secure, in large part because the public has placed a high level of trust and confidence in the Home Team, and also do their part to uphold law and order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This compact between Singaporeans and the Home Team is important and extends to the online domain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I spoke at the Smart Nation and Digital Government Group (SNDGG) COS debate about the digital social compact.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Within our security social compact, the Government enacts laws and policies, giving due consideration to all parties who have a stake.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We earn the public's trust by enforcing laws in a fair and transparent manner, and by consistently delivering good safety and security outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the online space, the Government does not set out to dictate or curtail the adoption of technology or use of online platforms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, we have a duty to protect our citizens from online harms, the same way we deal with threats in the physical domain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The measures we take must be reasonable and calibrated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As for the individual, we have a part to play by being alert and vigilant, and by looking out for the vulnerable amongst us, who may be more susceptible to crimes carried out online.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Vikram Nair asked for an update on legislation to target online criminal harms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Online harms are constantly evolving and take various forms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They include falsehoods, foreign interference and inappropriate sexual abuse material.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Online mediums are also exploited to incite violence, carry out scams at scale and traffic drugs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is a growing international consensus for rules to combat online harms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, jurisdictions such as the UK, the European Union (EU), Germany and Australia have introduced or proposed new laws to regulate the online space.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the years, the Government has taken steps to deal with different types of harmful online content and behaviours.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We introduced the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA) and the Foreign Interference Countermeasures Act (FICA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Broadcasting Act was recently amended to deal with harms that impact user safety, such as suicide and self-harm, cyberbullying and content likely to undermine racial and religious harmony.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We can also block access to egregious content on online communications services, including social media platforms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is online content which are criminal in their own right, or content which facilitate or abet crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include syndicated crimes, such as scams, online incitement of mass public disorder, and malicious cyber activities, such as phishing and the distribution of malware.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have been monitoring these developments closely and intend to update our suite of legislation to better protect our people.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes powers to stop or remove online communications that would facilitate crimes in the physical world, such as inciting violence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, it will increase the scope of entities we can act against.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will cover all mediums of online communication through which criminal activities could be conducted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, it will introduce levers that deal more effectively with the nature of online criminal harms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This legislation will also apply to other malicious cyber activities, like phishing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, MHA continues to monitor closely one specific type of online harm, that of online gambling.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Members know, gambling is prohibited unless licensed or exempted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This applies whether gambling takes place online or physically.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is especially as the lines between gambling and gaming have become blurred.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Take the example of video games with loot boxes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The loot box within the game must be entirely free of charge to play.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Otherwise, the game must not contain monetisation facilities; meaning that players cannot exchange the virtual prizes for real-world payouts, such as money or merchandise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It ensures we safeguard against gambling inducement, rather than gaming.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to monitor the effectiveness of our gambling legislation and update our regulatory approach where needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Beyond legislation, the Home Team must constantly enhance our capabilities to respond to evolving threats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the returns from our transformation efforts and how we will make future investments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue such investments to improve our operations and reduce our reliance on manpower.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The results can be seen through how the Home Team has been transforming in four areas: Processes, Platforms, People and Partnerships – four "Ps".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the years, we have used automation and biometrics to make our immigration clearance more efficient.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, Singaporeans who travel through Changi Airport are familiar with the automated immigration clearance gates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Following successful proof-of-concept trials, ICA and Home Team Science and Technology Agency (HTX) are now working to introduce automated in-car clearance for car travellers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Travellers will remain seated in the car and self-scan their passport and biometrics to verify their identities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With automated clearance, we expect overall faster and more secure clearance for car travellers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It also reduces the manpower demand, which can be deployed to meet other needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked how technology helped tackle domestic and transnational crime and aid our ground operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have invested in new technology platforms, such as those that improve incident response.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In this regard, the use of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) has been a game changer for the Home Team as it provides us with an eye in the sky that supplement ground officers and ground-based cameras.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, SPF deployed such systems for crowd management at events, including heartland celebrations of the National Day Parade and the year-end countdown in 2022.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: HTX is further pushing the boundaries by trialling a system that can be operated remotely from a centralised command and control centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will allow SPF and SCDF commanders to receive visuals of the scene even before our officers arrive, allowing them to better plan their responses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Technology has also supported our fight against scams, which are crimes that often have a transnational element.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Minister of State Sun will provide more details in her speech.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza rightly pointed out the challenging manpower situation, which is why we have redesigned our training.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, our built environment is becoming more complex for our firefighting and rescue operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The redeveloped Field Training Area at the Civil Defence Academy will host new infrastructure and stimulators that expand our training scenarios in an area nearly the size of three football fields.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team must also ensure that we have the specialised talent to enable our use of advanced technology, and Mr Murali Pillai asked how HTX has helped.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Beyond consolidating capabilities from across the Home Team, HTX has developed deep expertise in areas, ranging from biometrics to robotics and automation, that support the Home Team's unique needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The partnerships which HTX has forged, both with local research institutions and foreign counterparts, has enabled us to be at the forefront of new technological developments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So that it has enough talent, this year, HTX will be ramping up its recruitment and training of fresh science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) graduates from the universities as well as polytechnics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also include experienced professionals from the science, engineering and digital technology sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, our stakeholders and the public are ultimately who we serve.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Technology has enabled us to enhance the final "P" – partnerships that are essential to the Home Team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, SCDF's myResponder app has been key to helping to activate Community First Responders (CFRs), who are members of the public, to provide immediate assistance before our officers arrive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To better equip these responders to respond to minor fires, SCDF will start a new trial to place one fire extinguisher at the ground floor of every two Housing and Development Board (HDB) blocks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When fully implemented over five years, this will benefit 1.1 million HDB households.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Murali also asked about the lessons we have learnt from our transformation journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One key lesson is that transformation does not just come about by deploying more technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must also streamline our processes, train our officers with the relevant skills and make our partners a part of our transformation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, the Home Team transforms its capabilities so that it can continue to respond effectively to a wide range of threats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some, like terrorist attacks, we hope to never have to respond to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we must be prepared nonetheless, and realistic exercises are one way we can achieve this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a valuable opportunity to validate our interagency responses and capabilities in a realistic setting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We certainly consider the ability of an applicant to integrate in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But unlike the Swiss system, we do not use a naturalisation test or interviews.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Sample questions for the Swiss naturalisation test can easily be found online.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One can learn the right answers that immigration authorities want to hear and not actually be integrated with locals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Interviews, if conducted at scale, will also be resource-intensive and uneven in quality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, in 2021, 41% of those with a migrant background felt that they were not perceived as Swiss.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a survey that was conducted by the Swiss themselves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are assessed together with their economic contributions, qualifications and age.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All applicants must also complete the Singapore Citizenship Journey before being granted citizenship.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This programme helps participants better appreciate our history and culture.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It was recently refreshed and enhanced, with content co-created with ordinary Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As to Mr Pritam Singh's call to publicise detailed criteria for assessing citizenship applications, let me restate the key reasons not to do so, which remain valid.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, detailed criteria can be abused to inflate an undeserving applicant's chances of success.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are applicants who submit false documents just to obtain immigration facilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This problem will be exacerbated if we publish the detailed criteria and applicants know exactly what areas they can game.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: ICA will have a harder time securing the integrity of our process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, we have unique sensitivities by virtue of history and geography.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, most of our PRs and new Singapore Citizens (SCs) come from neighbouring regions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We do not reveal our detailed criteria or disclose country-specific figures on our PR and SC population, as this information could be misinterpreted or misused by others to stir up bilateral and domestic sensitivities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Singh spoke about a points-based system and asked why the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) publicises its criteria for the assessment of Employment Passes (EPs) whereas we do not for PRs and SCs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For most EPs, the stay in Singapore will come to an end.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For PRs and SCs, this is far less likely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must, therefore, also consider how they impact our demographic make-up and social fabric over the long term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Because of the permanent nature of PR and SC facilities, the need to guard against gaming is also greater.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, allow me now to speak in Mandarin.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Chairman, Singapore remains one of the safest countries in the world, in large part because the public has placed a high level of trust and confidence in the Home Team, and do their part to uphold law and order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we cannot take our peaceful state of affairs for granted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team must anticipate and deal with emerging and evolving threats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We continue to put in place new laws and policies to improve Singapore's safety and security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One such area is our approach towards online harms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will build on our existing laws and strengthen our ability to deal with online criminal activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes powers to stop or remove online communications that facilitate crimes in the physical world, such as inciting violence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team will also continue to enhance our capabilities and partner the public to keep Singapore safe.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, there are more than 130,000 CFRs today, who are members of the public that can provide immediate assistance to minor fire and cardiac arrest cases before our officers arrive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To better equip CFRs to respond to minor fires, SCDF will be embarking on a new trial to place one fire extinguisher at the ground floor of every two HDB blocks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's success in meeting safety and security threats relies on the collective effort of the Home Team and the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team will continue to do our utmost to live up to the trust and confidence Singaporeans have placed in us, so that Singapore will remain a safe and secure home for all of us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, the Home Team continues to do well in keeping our streets safe.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: However, terrorism poses a serious threat to our security.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about efforts to combat terrorism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: International cooperation is critical to tackling terrorism and terrorism financing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We work closely with overseas counterparts to share intelligence on potential terror threats and conduct joint operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to enhance collaboration through international platforms, such as the Financial Action Task Force and INTERPOL.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Within Singapore, we have implemented structures and processes to take swift action against terrorism financing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This includes the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism Steering Committee, which coordinates efforts amongst Government agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We also work closely with private sector partners under the Countering the Financing of Terrorism Operational Group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This workgroup facilitates round-the-clock investigative collaboration, allowing us to investigate terrorism financing expeditiously.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Youth radicalisation cases have increased significantly in recent years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked about measures to address youth radicalisation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This includes workshops to train school counsellors to identify signs of radicalisation and on early intervention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The upcoming Online Criminal Harms Act announced by the Second Minister earlier will also give us powers to direct takedowns of online content facilitating radicalisation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As the threat of terrorism in Singapore remains high, we will continue to enhance our operational capabilities and expand our outreach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Globally, drug use continues to rise, posing challenges to keeping Singapore drug-free.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Locally, while the drug situation remains under control, we are concerned with drug abuse amongst youths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: While most youths support a tough stance against drugs, some younger Singaporeans take a more permissive attitude, especially towards cannabis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked how we are preventing drug abuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to strengthen our harm prevention approach to combat drug abuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our first line of defence against drugs is a well-informed public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Derrick Goh asked about preventive drug education (PDE) for youths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The CNB will expand PDE efforts in schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Moving forward, CNB is working with the Ministry of Education (MOE) to ensure all primary and secondary schools conduct at least one PDE programme annually.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: With TikTok becoming increasingly popular amongst youths, CNB launched its TikTok account last year, which regularly posts short videos of our drug enforcement efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about sensitising the public to the threat of drug liberalisation globally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB highlights trends of concern in the global drug situation through various communication channels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As part of the #CNBPerspectives Series launched in 2022, CNB took to Facebook and Instagram to share worrying trends from the World Drug Report 2022.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In fact, I also posted things relating to this to support their effort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These include the increase of cannabis-use disorders in jurisdictions which legalise cannabis for non-medical use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We also educate our anti-drug abuse advocates about the increasingly permissive views other countries have towards drugs and train them to speak up against drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The second pillar of our anti-drug strategy is tough laws and robust enforcement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To deter Singaporeans and PRs from abusing drugs overseas, CNB has stepped up enforcement at the checkpoints with the deployment of Saliva Test Kits from January this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These kits, like the one I am holding here – they are light and compact.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They offer a more efficient way to detect drug abusers at the checkpoints.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This month, CNB and Police started trialling joint roadblock operations to detect drug abusers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked about enforcement against New Psychoactive Substances (NPS) and vaping.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The speed and breadth at which NPS variants have appeared have often outpaced authorities' ability to control them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This will empower CNB to take swift enforcement actions against illicit activities involving NPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Enforcement against vaping will be addressed at the Ministry of Health (MOH)'s COS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The third pillar of our anti-drug strategy is enhancing rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked about efforts to reduce drug recidivism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB recently reviewed its drug supervision regime and has deployed suitable officers to take on specialist roles in supervision to enhance the rehabilitation process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As I had announced last year, CNB has been piloting Community Supervision Sessions, in short, CoSS, since 2019, where supervision officers help supervisees address financial, housing and other rehabilitation needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A supervisee who has benefited from CoSS is 46-year-old Mr Aidil.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: After his release from the Drug Rehabilitation Centre (DRC) in 2021, Aidil was afraid of not being able to find a suitable job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Through CoSS sessions, Aidil was given career guidance and advice on his rehabilitation needs by his supervision officer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: With this support, Aidil landed a part-time job within five months of his release.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about support for desistors with drug-abusing pasts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The SPS has enhanced its Psychology-based Correctional Programmes (PCPs) to be more targeted for repeated drug abusers during their in-care period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These PCPs will cater more time to address negative attitudes and improve emotional regulation, as both factors contribute to repeated drug use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked about efforts to reduce recidivism, and Mr Patrick Tay and Dr Tan Wu Meng asked about improving the employability of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We must work with community partners to offer offenders and drug abusers an ecosystem of support, starting from when they enter our prisons and DRCs, and continuing to do so after their release.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: First, by enhancing their skills and employment outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Gainful employment allows ex-offenders to be financially independent and reduces risks of re-offending.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2023, SPS and YRSG will continue to work with partners to help ex-offenders upskill and boost their longer-term career progression.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In collaboration with the Institute of Technical Education (ITE), SPS has set up education hubs to enrol more inmate students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2023, SPS will work with ITE to run more short courses, such as the Computer Maintenance course, following positive reviews.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I am pleased to announce that YRSG is launching the YR Sandbox initiative to develop new career options in emerging sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: YRSG will work with industry partners to hire releasing inmates and provide on-the-job training or work-study programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Potential sectors include skilled sectors like Digital, Built Environment and Agri-Tech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This new initiative complements TAP & Grow – TAP meaning "Train and Place".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This scheme provides inmates with industry training in prison and potential job placement with a partner employer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: TAP & Grow has been launched in the Precision Engineering, Media and Logistics and Wholesale sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It will provide time-limited wage offsets to encourage employers to hire ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Currently, about two-thirds of ex-offenders secure employment within six months of release.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We hope to improve this and will raise awareness of the UEC and other available support amongst employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng asked about recognition for inclusive employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2022, over 200 employers, community partners, ex-offenders and volunteers were recognised for their contributions towards second chances through the Yellow Ribbon Awards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Second, by strengthening pro-social support in the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The community, including ex-offenders themselves and their family plays a critical role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about enhancing post-release mentorship.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I am pleased to announce that SPS has piloted a new scheme for volunteers to assist in the case management of selected supervisees emplaced on Community-Based Programmes (CBPs).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Volunteer Case Officers will guide the supervisees towards a pro-social life during and beyond the CBP.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: SPS is working with community partners to launch the Desistor Network in April this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Desistors who have stayed clear of crime and drugs will serve as mentors to recently released ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This will also strengthen desistors' sense of self as contributing members of the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked about follow-ups from the CARE Network Summit 2022 and expanding YRSG's role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: YRSG will continue to work closely with SPS and community partners via the CARE Network to tackle long-term recidivism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: From 2023, the CARE Network will tap on the Desistor Network to co-opt desistors in planning and conducting programmes for ex-offenders.
